name: Rubel paper offset lithography
description: A lithographic press transfers an inked image to an intermediate rubber surface before printing paper.

impact.note: Offset transfer became the usual way printed matter was made in many countries; cheaper, sharper printing rather than a new ability, with improved presses following.

date.basis: Date or stated historical interval in cited source; see caveats.

events.statement: A rotary offset press built by Ira Rubel operated in his New York plant.

evidence.supports: Smithsonian describes Rubel’s paper offset press and operation in 1904.

contributions.resource: Purchased the press for use in San Francisco.

evidence.supports: Smithsonian documents the 1905 sale and price.

earliest_record.rationale: Earliest dated witness established by the cited source for this scoped record, not a claim of global first.

measures.money_context: Nominal 1905 transaction; not a general retail price.

links.statement: Offset printing applied lithographic printing through an intermediate surface.
links.scope: Lithographic process lineage, not a claim of direct personal contact with Senefelder.

evidence.supports: The catalog describes the development of lithography and offset transfer.

caveats: European tin printers had already used intermediate rubber cylinders; this record is a paper-printing implementation and does not claim global first for all offset printing.

research.note: Initial sourced research; independent review pending. Independent review checked Smithsonian’s 1904 operation and the 1905 $5,500 sale; later San Francisco operation began in 1907.
